positions.label: Afternoon of July 2: Stuart takes position on Ewell's left (Lee); no hour is recorded

support.quote: He reached Carlisle on July 1, [...] He arrived in the afternoon of the following day, and took position on General Ewell's left

witness.name: Robert E. Lee
witness.role: General commanding the Army of Northern Virginia

phrases: He arrived in the afternoon of the following day

support.note: Lee's full report of January 1864 (p. 305 starts his shorter report of 31 July 1863, which gives no hour). The sentence before it says Stuart reached Carlisle on July 1, so the following day is July 2. Lee does not say how he learned the hour.

support.quote: My advance reached Gettysburg July 2, just in time to thwart a move of the enemy's cavalry

witness.name: J. E. B. Stuart
witness.role: Major General commanding the Cavalry Division, Army of Northern Virginia

support.note: Stuart's own report (20 August 1863): the day, no hour. 'My advance' was Hampton's brigade at Hunterstown; Stuart himself 'took my position that day on the York and Heidlersburg roads'.

support.quote: Stuart himself, with Fitz Lee's and [...] commands, reached [...] on the afternoon of the 2d

witness.name: Henry B. McClellan
witness.role: Major, Stuart's assistant adjutant general and chief of staff; biographer of Stuart

support.note: Stuart's chief of staff, 22 years later. The words 'took position on the Confederate left' follow Lee's report closely, so this is counted with Lee's, not as a second line. The OCR damages two words (Chambliss, Gettysburg); the quote skips them.

support.quote: Toward the afternoon of July 2, Stuart, with Fitz Lee's and Chambliss's brigades, took position on the extreme left flank

witness.name: George Gordon Meade (the general's grandson, editor) and his father George Meade
witness.role: editors and narrators of Life and Letters of George Gordon Meade

support.note: A narrative by non-participants in the volume of 1913, no source named; it puts Fitz Lee's and Chambliss's brigades with Stuart on the left 'toward the afternoon'. 'Toward the afternoon' is an unusual phrase and is read here only as 'in the afternoon'.

support.quote: reported in person, late in the afternoon of the 2d

witness.name: Edward Porter Alexander
witness.role: Colonel, chief of artillery of Longstreet's corps; author of Military Memoirs of a Confederate

phrases: late in the afternoon of the 2d

support.note: Alexander was on the field with Longstreet's corps on July 2 but not at Lee's side when Stuart reported; he gives Lee's reproach 'Well, General, you are here at last' and the hour. Also says the column 'arrived that afternoon'. 1907, 44 years later.

support.page_note: the text carries no page marks and the passage is not tied to a printed page here
support.quote: had arrived on the left, with two of his brigades, before sunset

witness.name: Douglas Southall Freeman
witness.role: historian, biographer of Lee (not a participant)

support.note: Freeman writes this in the account of Lee's decision on the night of July 2 and his footnote reads 'McClellan, 332', so he repeats McClellan (who follows Lee) and is counted in that line; it fixes only an upper bound (Stuart on the left with two brigades before sunset, about 19:32).

positions.label: Evening: the cavalry Stuart accompanied "joined General Lee on the evening of the second day" (Taylor, 1877)

support.quote: only joined General Lee on the evening of the second day

witness.name: Walter H. Taylor
witness.role: Lieutenant Colonel, adjutant general on Lee's staff

phrases: on the evening of the second day

support.note: The sentence is about the cavalry force Stuart accompanied ('That portion which General Stuart accompanied ... only joined General Lee on the evening of the second day'), in a passage on the strength of the armies: it may date the brigades' joining the army, not Stuart's own call on Lee, and is not read as the latter. Reprinted in the Southern Historical Society Papers vol. 4, 1877 (same author, counted once). 14 years later.

support.quote: It was the evening of July 2 when he finally reached the main army

witness.name: James H. Kidd
witness.role: Union cavalry officer, Michigan Cavalry Brigade (Custer)

support.note: Union officer's address at the Michigan monuments, 26 years later; he was not with Stuart and gives no source.

inference.step: Taylor writes that Stuart only joined General Lee on the evening of the second day and Kidd that he reached the main army in the evening; read as the time the cavalry Stuart accompanied (the brigades) joined the army; Taylor's subject is that cavalry force, not Stuart's call on Lee, and Kidd's is Stuart himself

reason_not_chosen.text: Told 14 and 26 years later, no clock; Lee's report of 1864 says afternoon. Taylor speaks of the cavalry Stuart accompanied, so it may date the brigades, which a sundown fight does not contradict.

positions.label: Evening, about sundown: Hampton's brigade fights at Hunterstown (a different event)

support.quote: Was attacked by Stuart, Hampton, and Lee at sundown near Hunterstown

witness.name: Judson Kilpatrick
witness.role: Brigadier General commanding the Third Division, Cavalry Corps (Union)

support.note: Kilpatrick's report on the Third Division, dated 10 August 1863. 'Sundown' is not a clock reading; sunset at Gettysburg was 19:32.

support.quote: Thursday evening, July 2, just before sunset, I was ordered to report [...] to General Hampton, at Hunt
support.note: His section was ordered to Hampton at Hunterstown 'just before sunset' and arrived at dusk, so Hampton was at Hunterstown before sunset. The date of the report (8 July) is read from the damaged heading of the text; the day digit was not checked on the page image.

support.quote: The brigade was stationed on July 2, at Hunterstown, 5 miles to the east of Gettysburg, when orders came from General Stuart

witness.name: Wade Hampton
witness.role: Brigadier General commanding the brigade (Confederate cavalry)

support.note: Hampton's report of 13 August 1863 on Gettysburg: the brigade was at Hunterstown when Stuart's order to move up came, so Stuart was already giving orders for the left before the fight. No hour.

reason_not_chosen.text: It dates the fight at Hunterstown (sundown, 19:32), not Stuart's arrival: Hampton was stationed there before it. It supports the plan's evening for brigades only as the hour of a battle.

value.text: on the morning of the 2d of July

support.quote: Hampton reached Hunterstown on the morning of the 2d of July

witness.name: Henry B. McClellan
witness.role: Major, Stuart's assistant adjutant general and chief of staff; biographer of Stuart

phrases: on the morning of the 2d of July

support.note: Stuart's chief of staff, 1885, from the text around Hampton's report; the report itself gives no hour for reaching Hunterstown.

positions.label: Late afternoon: Hampton's brigade reaches Hunterstown (Kidd, 1889)

support.quote: Kilpatrick reached the inside of the union lines in the vicinity of Gettysburg late in the afternoon, at about the same hour that Hampton, with Stuart's leading Brigade, arrived in Hunterstown

witness.name: James H. Kidd
witness.role: Union cavalry officer, Michigan Cavalry Brigade (Custer)

positions.label: Jenkins's brigade: with Ewell since June; under Stuart only on July 3 (a different event)

support.quote: wounded the day previous, before reporting to me

witness.name: J. E. B. Stuart
witness.role: Major General commanding the Cavalry Division, Army of Northern Virginia

phrases: wounded the day previous, before reporting to me

support.note: On July 3 Stuart's command was 'increased by the addition of Jenkins' brigade' (p. 697); Jenkins was wounded the day before, before reporting to Stuart.

support.quote: General Jenkins, with his cavalry, who accompanied General Ewell

witness.name: Robert E. Lee
witness.role: General commanding the Army of Northern Virginia

support.note: Lee's report of 31 July 1863, on the advance into Pennsylvania in June.

support.quote: only the commands of Generals Imboden and Jenkins had been with the army from the time of crossing the Potomac, and they accom- [...] panied General Ewell

witness.name: Walter H. Taylor
witness.role: Lieutenant Colonel, adjutant general on Lee's staff

phrases: Jenkins had been with the army from the time of crossing the Potomac

inference.step: Lee (July 1863) and Taylor (1877) put Jenkins's cavalry with Ewell from the crossing of the Potomac; Stuart says it was added to his command on July 3 and Jenkins was wounded the day before; so Jenkins did not arrive with Stuart on July 2 and the plan's evening does not describe it

reason_not_chosen.text: Not an arrival time: it says Jenkins's brigade was already with the army and came under Stuart on July 3, so it needs no arrival of its own on July 2.

weighing.summary: Every record agrees on the day, July 2; none gives a clock reading for Stuart or his brigades. The only official statement of the period is Lee's: 'arrived in the afternoon'. Writers who give a more exact moment are later: Alexander (late in the afternoon, when Stuart reported in person), Taylor (evening, for the cavalry Stuart accompanied), Kidd (evening), Freeman (before sunset). Noon to 13:00 and mid-afternoon are in no source and early afternoon is not in any either. The plan's pair (Stuart early afternoon, brigades evening) mixes events: Hampton's brigade stood at Hunterstown and fought at sundown, Fitz Lee and Chambliss were with Stuart in the afternoon, and Jenkins was with Ewell. Afternoon, from the best-classed writing, is the default; its upper end (late afternoon, before sunset) is the same as the evening of the later writers.
weighing.who: Lee commanded the army and wrote of his own cavalry's arrival; Stuart and Hampton wrote of their own movements and give no hour; Kilpatrick and Green wrote of the fight at Hunterstown they were in. Taylor was Lee's adjutant, McClellan Stuart's chief of staff, Alexander Longstreet's artillery chief: all were on the field but none says how he knew the hour. Kidd was a Union officer and Meade's volume and Freeman are histories.
weighing.when: Stuart (20 Aug 1863), Hampton (13 Aug), Kilpatrick (10 Aug), Green (8 Jul) and Lee (31 Jul 1863; 20 Jan 1864) wrote within 7 months, the best class of writing. McClellan (1885), Taylor (1877), Alexander (1907), Kidd (1889), Meade's volume (1913) and Freeman (1935) wrote 14 to 72 years after and rank below them (reminiscence and history).
weighing.where: Lee was with the army on Seminary Ridge and Stuart took position on the left; Hampton was at Hunterstown. Taylor was with Lee; his sentence is about the cavalry force Stuart accompanied, so it may date the brigades, not Stuart's call on Lee; Kidd and Freeman were not with Stuart.
weighing.how_knew: Stuart and Hampton knew their own movements and say no hour; Lee relied on Stuart's report and what he saw, and does not say how he fixed the afternoon. The later writers give no source, except Freeman by footnote.
weighing.clock: None gives a clock reading, so the 20-minute difference between the two clocks (never applied) does not matter. 'Sundown' (Kilpatrick, Union) and 'just before sunset' (Green, Confederate) both point to about 19:32, sunset at Gettysburg.
weighing.independence: Lee's report, McClellan, the Meade volume and Freeman are counted as one line (McClellan and Meade follow Lee's words about taking position on the left; Freeman's footnote reads 'McClellan, 332'); Alexander, Taylor, Kidd, Kilpatrick, Green and Hampton are separate. Afternoon is carried by two lines (Lee with the writers that repeat him, and Alexander); evening by two memoirs (Taylor for the cavalry, Kidd for Stuart, one Union). Lee's 'afternoon' also stands beside the Hunterstown fight that Kilpatrick puts at sundown, so it is a loose word. So the default is weighted, not settled: the afternoon and the evening are compatible if Stuart reached the left in the afternoon and the brigades or his call on Lee came late; the records do not say that.

source_panel_text: Afternoon of July 2: Lee's report says Stuart arrived in the afternoon and took position on Ewell's left; Stuart gives the day, no hour. No record gives noon, 1 p.m. or mid-afternoon. Taylor (1877, for the cavalry Stuart accompanied) and Kidd (1889) say evening; Alexander says Stuart reported to Lee late in the afternoon. Hampton fought at Hunterstown at sundown. Nine other values stay listed.

pdf_default.note: The afternoon holds for Stuart himself (Lee's report), but early afternoon has no source and Alexander has him reporting late in the afternoon. Evening holds as the hour of Hampton's fight at Hunterstown and, on Taylor's sentence about the cavalry, possibly for the brigades; Fitz Lee and Chambliss came with Stuart in the afternoon, and Jenkins was already with Ewell.

what_would_change_it: A report, letter or diary written on or near July 2-3, 1863 by Lee, a member of his staff, Stuart, Fitz Lee, Chambliss or a courier that gives a clock reading for Stuart's arrival on the left or his report to Lee (for instance Lee's headquarters papers, Fitz Lee's report, Chambliss's report, Venable's or Marshall's recollections, or Stuart's staff diaries). A narrower hour would split the afternoon; a reading before 15:00 would make early afternoon the value, and an hour at dusk would make Taylor's evening the better reading.
